what: Dolby Laboratories licenses audio and imaging technology. Device makers pay Dolby to use its sound and picture formats — Dolby Atmos for immersive audio, Dolby Vision for high dynamic range video — and studios, streaming services and cinemas use them to produce and show content.
customers: Consumer electronics manufacturers building televisions, phones, laptops, soundbars and headphones; film studios, streaming services and cinema operators; and car makers adding Atmos to vehicles.
money: Royalties from device makers and content producers using Dolby formats.
Cinema processors, imaging products and Dolby Cinema arrangements.
moat: The strength is a standard that both sides of a market have adopted: studios master content in Dolby formats because devices support them, and device makers support the formats because content exists. Neither side moves first to abandon it. That two-sided lock-in is why a technology licensing business can sustain high margins without manufacturing anything.
risks: Revenue has been essentially flat at about $1.3B for four years, so growth is the central problem.
Royalty revenue depends on device shipments, and smartphone and television unit volumes are mature.
Only three analysts cover the stock, so the $71.67 average target rests on very thin coverage.
Device makers have both the incentive and occasionally the ability to adopt royalty-free alternatives, and a large manufacturer deciding to do so would matter.
The shares trade at about 20.3 times earnings, which is not cheap for a business with no revenue growth.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $359.9M on $1.4B of revenue, at about 14.1 times free cash flow, with a net margin of about 18.1%.
Cash of $623.4M against $45.8M of debt means a large share of the market value is net cash.
Licensing requires almost no capital: the same technology is licensed to every manufacturer at negligible incremental cost.
Dolby Atmos in cars is a genuinely new royalty stream growing from nothing.
Two-sided adoption by studios and device makers makes the standard very difficult to displace.
watch: Royalty revenue per device category, particularly automotive and Atmos. Device volumes are mature, so growth has to come from new categories or higher royalties per device.
view: Dolby owns a standard, which is one of the best things a technology company can own. Film studios master their soundtracks in Dolby formats because consumer devices support them; device makers support the formats because the content exists. Neither side has an incentive to move first, and the cost of being the one manufacturer whose television cannot play a Dolby Vision film is far higher than the royalty. That two-sided lock-in is why a company that manufactures almost nothing earns an 18% net margin.

The financial profile follows from the model. Licensing the same technology to every manufacturer costs essentially nothing incrementally, so the revenue converts to cash at a high rate — $360 million of free cash flow on $1.4 billion of revenue — and the balance sheet holds $623 million of cash against $46 million of debt. A meaningful share of the market value is simply money.

The problem is that revenue has sat at about $1.3 billion for four years, and the reason is arithmetic rather than competitive. Royalties come from device shipments, and smartphone and television unit volumes are mature — the world is not buying many more televisions than it did five years ago. Growth therefore has to come from new categories or from charging more per device, and the most interesting of those is automotive: Dolby Atmos in cars is a royalty stream that started at zero and is growing.

The risk worth taking seriously is a large manufacturer deciding the royalty is not worth paying and adopting a royalty-free alternative. Standards look permanent until a dominant player with its own ecosystem decides otherwise, and this has happened in other licensing businesses. At 20.3 times earnings and 14.1 times free cash flow, with three analysts covering a $5.1 billion company, the price assumes the standard holds and growth resumes. The first assumption I would accept; the second needs the new categories to deliver.
bull: Automotive Atmos and new device categories restart royalty growth while a two-sided standard keeps manufacturers paying, on a net-cash balance sheet at 14 times free cash flow.
bear: Mature device volumes keep revenue flat indefinitely, or a dominant manufacturer adopts a royalty-free alternative and the standard’s grip loosens.
